answer.rationale: I'm pulling c1 (incumbent renewal kept integration stable across two cycles, no migration work, no delivery interruption) and c6 (multi-year commitments with the incumbent unlocked volume pricing and cut unit cost without narrowing service scope). Together these give me the clearest read on whether—and how—to push the incumbent rather than rip-and-replace. Given finance's 18% cut mandate, the incumbent's refusal to reopen price this cycle, the 14-day contract cliff with no auto-renew, and the line running at 94% of committed volume with no buffer, the cost-down pressure is real but the delivery-risk side is just as binding. Switching primary vendors (memory_c2) saved money last time but onboarding was 'quick' and invoicing 'accurate'—that's encouraging, but switching under a 14-day cliff with a line already at 94% is the exact scenario c1 warns against (no migration work, no interruption to scheduled deliveries). Adding a second source (memory_c3) is a structural resilience lever, not a same-cycle cost lever, and I only get one decision this cycle. Deferring (memory_c5) preserved budget flexibility in another context but here it collides with a hard expiry and no auto-renew—deferral here isn't flexibility, it's lapse. That leaves negotiate_terms as the primary move: push the incumbent toward the volume-pricing / multi-year structure that c6 shows actually moved unit cost last time, while leaning on c1's record that the relationship has earned enough trust across two renewal cycles to absorb a longer commitment without service erosion. If terms can't be moved, the fallback shifts to a second source add, but I want the incumbent negotiation on the table first because it best satisfies 'minimize TCO without increasing delivery risk.' Memory c4 (renegotiation at renewal recovered real margin) is adjacent and tempting to pull, but c6 already covers the multi-year/margin recovery ground and I want to keep one verification slot in reserve.
